column1: # DRAFT (not executed; see README.md). G2 phase 2: the validation verb.
# WHY THESE ARE DRAFTED RATHER THAN LANDED. Both runners execute every
# row of every test/spec/*.tsv file, with no skip list -- a property the
# Go runner is deliberately proud of. A `vet` row therefore cannot
# become executable until `vet` exists in BOTH ports, which is phase 4.
# The engine landed in TypeScript first (ADR-001: TypeScript is
# canonical, the Go port follows), so its behaviour is pinned by
# ts/test/vet.test.ts today and by these rows when the port lands.
# THE ENCODING, settled by probing the engine rather than by argument.
# Three candidate encodings failed adversarial review before this one;
# what rules them out is recorded in the design document under "What the
# spec suite can actually pin". The surviving shape:
#   name <TAB> vet <TAB> schema <TAB> data <TAB> expect
# FIVE columns, not four. Both runners already tolerate extra columns
# (they read the first four and ignore the rest), so a `vet` arm reading
# a fifth is additive rather than a format change. The alternative --
# packing two documents into the single src cell with a separator --
# founders on the same rock as the compact finding summary: no
# punctuation is safe, because a quoted map key may contain any
# character.
# `expect` is a JSON object, encoded with the serialiser pair the suite
# already holds to byte parity (exactJSON / json.Encoder):
#   {"verdict":"invalid","truncated":false,"findings":[{...}]}
# MESSAGE TEXT IS EXCLUDED from the golden, deliberately. Codes are
# contractual across the ports and prose is not -- both runners say so
# at the `errc` site, and test/spec/divergent.tsv repeats it -- so a
# whole-report byte golden would silently promote every message string
# to a cross-port contract this repository refuses to make. The
# `message` field is asserted by substring in the per-port tests
# instead, the way `err` rows already work.
# SITES carry `file`, `row`, `col` and `role`. The files are named by
# the runner (`schema` and `data`), not by a path, so the golden does
# not depend on where the suite is checked out.
# Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>schema<TAB>data<TAB>expect
vet-valid
vet-invalid-kind
# Residue is INCOMPLETE, not invalid: the data does not yet satisfy the
# truth, as against never being able to. Bare vet is strict, so this is
# a failing verdict; --partial opts out.
vet-incomplete
# A schema that does not stand up on its own is never blamed on data.
vet-schema-error
vet-data-unparseable
# The data site is listed first: it is the thing to fix. Roles come from
# provenance, not from NilVal's primary/secondary heuristic, which is
# source-order reasoning within ONE document and says nothing useful
# when one side is a schema and the other is data.
vet-closed-key
# expected/actual come from the constraint algebra's own details, so
# G1's canonical bound syntax is what a repair loop is handed.
vet-constraint-alternatives
# The author's message from Band B rides the finding as `note`.
vet-must-note
# A path is not delimiter-safe, which is why the whole finding list is
# JSON rather than a compact code@path summary.
vet-path-with-space
# Vet sorts its own findings. The underlying walk follows raw key order
# and the two hosts disagree about that, so an unsorted report could
# never be in cross-port parity.
vet-sorted-by-data-site
vet-truncated
# The anchor and the closed flag are options rather than source, so
# these rows need the option column the runner arm will read from the
# expect object's "opts" key -- the one piece of this encoding that is
# NOT yet probed, because the TypeScript engine takes options as an
# argument and no runner passes them yet. Recorded here so the phase-4
# port does not rediscover it.
vet-at-subtree
vet-closed-anchor
vet-partial-allows-residue
